newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: FOCUS - BEARISH BOURSE GIVES LITHUANIAN DEALERS THE BLUES.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BEARISH BOURSE GIVES LITHUANIAN DEALERS THE BLUES.

text.p: Lithuania's bearish bourse has most Lithuanian dealers singing the blues, but they remain up beat about the struggling exchange's long-term prospects.
A brief survey of five Lithuanian brokerage houses conducted by Reuters found dealers divided over when they think prices and activity will pick up and the general mood was gloomy.
The most optimistic forecast saw prices rising slowly next week while the most cautious put prices up at the end of summer. One dealer was unsure and two saw slight gains in two to four weeks' time.
However, there was a consensus that things will start rolling by autumn at the latest as serious portflio investors come to the market.
Shares went on a wild bull-run in January, with the Litin A index, which tracks the bourse's most active listings, surging to 3,242.25, over double its late October value.
Things have been mostly down hill ever since, with the index stumbling 158.89 points on Thursday to 2,219.55.
On the bright side, the index is still over a third higher than its October level - an impressive gain even in today's world of soaring share prices.
Dealers say that January's rapid climb was fueled by domestic buyers and was for the most speculative and not based on a serious analysis of the market.
The January events were also touched off by a switch to equities from debt in response to falling Treasury bill yields.
"January's situation was not based on any careful examination of companies," said one dealer.
"Today's situation has not been helped by disappointing first quarter results," he added.
"Serious investors are only examining the market now...it won't pick up before summer," said Kestutis Kupsys of brokerage firm Mendes Prior Europe.
His comments were echoed by other dealers, who said that long-term foreign investors were expected to arrive in the next few months.
A group of senior fund managers visited Lithuania last week on a fact finding-mission.
Members of the delegation interviewed by Reuters said that Lithuania's equities market had a lot of potential for future growth and lucrative returns.
The government's commitment to selling off attractive state enterprises, a good macroeconomic climate, political stability and bargain prices bode well for the future.
But in the short-term, dealers see no reason to change their gloomy tune.
Brokerage house Suprema is the exception to the rule, though its dealers are far from bullish about the short-term.
"Prices may begin rising slightly next week simply because they are so low right now," said Arvydas Jacikevicius of Suprema.
